Ibn ʿĀshūr says the direct reading admonishes polytheists."}, {"id": "75:21/q05/p2", "position": "Human beings generally, whose natural haste exposes them to this fault, with divinely protected exceptions.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says singular ‘the human’ denotes the species and the plural generalizes rebuke. {"id": "75:21/q06", "question": "What drives people to leave the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "The notes explain abandonment through immediate desire and haste, disbelief in the future, or aversion to the consequences of one's deeds; some combine these causes.", "positions": [{"id": "75:21/q06/p1", "position": "Attachment to immediate pleasure and human haste displace thought and work for the Hereafter, and can fuel denial.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī likens the two lives to rival co-wives: love of one blinds and deafens one to the other; he contrasts the Prophet's soul, urging obedience, with theirs, which urges fleeting gain. Al-Qāshānī, al-Ālūsī, al-Sāmarrāʾī, and al-Zamakhsharī as reported by al-Sāmarrāʾī connect this to human haste; al-Sāmarrāʾī cites 21:37. His report of al-Ālūsī adds delayed repentance, false hope, indulgence, and the wish to sin ahead (75:5). Ibn Kathīr says preoccupation with this world explains heedlessness, opposition to revelation, and denial of resurrection; Iṣlāḥī says conscience already testifies to Judgment, but luxuries and unwillingness to forgo present pleasure produce excuses. Al-Sāmarrāʾī likewise says the preference accounts for denial and turning away."}, {"id": "75:21/q06/p2", "position": "They believe in what is present but deny the future resurrection and its reward.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explicitly pairs belief in the present with denial of the future. Ibn Kathīr and Abū Ḥayyān describe a denier who rejects resurrection and therefore disregards its reward; the latter says he is concerned instead with perishable gain."}, {"id": "75:21/q06/p3", "position": "They hate the Hereafter because their own deeds will harm them there.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes their anticipated harmful outcome the reason for aversion and abandonment."}]}
{"id": "75:21/q07", "question": "What conduct does the verse condemn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:21/q07/p1", "position": "Worldly attachment becomes blameworthy when it displaces obedience and the Hereafter; worldly enjoyment with obedience is allowed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the two acts together deserve censure and cites 28:77 for enjoying worldly life while obeying revelation. Kur’an Yolu says blessings were created for people and cites 7:31–33; abandonment of the Hereafter because of love for them is censured. Junayd says pursuing and turning toward the world costs a person a share of the Hereafter. Al-Biqāʿī's rival co-wives image says love of one drives actions that distance one from the other; Qatāda notes exceptions whom God protects."}]}
{"id": "75:21/q08", "question": "How does the verse's wording sharpen the reproach?", "turns_on": "The notes identify different rhetorical devices in the wording rather than opposing interpretations.", "positions": [{"id": "75:21/q08/p1", "position": "The plural and direct address broaden and intensify the rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says plural address generalizes the charge despite the earlier singular human; al-Biqāʿī says the plural follows the collective sense of human. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say direct confrontation makes blame or admonition more forceful. Al-Ālūsī cites the proverb that a hide is reproached only while sound to underline how deeply worldly love resists admonition; he also says the second-person reading includes the listener. Al-Farrāʾ points to the Qurʾān's address shifts and compares 10:22."}, {"id": "75:21/q08/p2", "position": "The paired clauses use iḥtibāk, each supplying what the other leaves unstated.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says loving the present implies hatred of the Hereafter, while leaving the Hereafter implies turning to and taking the present."}]}
{"id": "75:21/q09", "question": "How does this accusation relate to the preceding instruction to the Prophet in 75:16–19?", "turns_on": "Whether 75:16–19 is only a parenthetical change of addressee or also supplies a thematic comparison about haste; al-Ālūsī separately rejects an allegation of textual alteration.", "positions": [{"id": "75:21/q09/p1", "position": "The instruction is an aside; the discourse now returns to deniers or humanity, and the charge is not addressed to the Prophet as a continuation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the discourse returns from addressing the Prophet to the earlier denier. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the instruction parenthetical and unrelated to the verses on either side. Iṣlāḥī calls it an aside about patience in piecemeal revelation before the original sequence resumes; Kur’an Yolu likewise sees a return to humanity and its denial of resurrection. Study Quran notes the shift from singular Prophet to plural humanity; Elmalılı notes a general address after the Prophet."}, {"id": "75:21/q09/p2", "position": "The insertion forms a purposeful link: haste in receiving revelation makes haste toward worldly ruin still more blameworthy.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the Prophet is lovingly guided away from haste and told to wait, then the address generalizes to humanity; if haste is barred in receiving the healing, merciful Qurʾān (75:16), it is still less fitting in pursuit of depravity. Al-Ālūsī rejects a hostile inference from the passage's placement that the Qurʾān was altered, saying scholars answered it."}, {"id": "75:21/q09/p3", "position": "The intervening tongue prohibition is irrelevant and proves textual alteration.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this claim to some heretics and early extremist Rāfiḍīs, rejects it, and says scholars have answered it."}]}
{"id": "75:21/q10", "question": "What earlier claim or excuse does this verse answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:21/q10/p1", "position": "It exposes worldly desire as the real reason behind denial of resurrection and false excuses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the explicit charge develops 75:5 after 75:16–19 interrupts, making reproach progressively stronger. {"id": "75:26/q01", "question": "What does kallā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether kallā rebukes disbelief and worldly attachment or affirms the certainty of death; the rebuke is variously tied to prior denial or preference for the immediate life.", "positions": [{"id": "75:26/q01/p1", "position": "It rebukes and warns people, especially for preferring this world and denying what lies beyond it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj calls it a warning to desist from deeds leading to punishment; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr relate it to preferring immediate life. {"id": "75:26/q02", "question": "What governs the conditional idhā?", "turns_on": "Which part of the surrounding passage completes or governs the time clause.", "positions": [{"id": "75:26/q02/p1", "position": "Its governor may be baṣīra.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās names baṣīra as one possible governor."}, {"id": "75:26/q02/p2", "position": "Its governor may be balaghat; the answer comes later.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās explicitly gives this alternative and says the answer then occurs later in the passage."}, {"id": "75:26/q02/p3", "position": "It attaches to the implied predicate 'the journey is to your Lord.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies this later predicate as the construction to which 'when it reaches' attaches."}]}
{"id": "75:26/q03", "question": "What reaches the tarāqī?", "turns_on": "Whether the unstated feminine referent is the soul or the dying person's final breath.", "positions": [{"id": "75:26/q03/p1", "position": "The soul or spirit reaches them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās specifies the disbeliever's soul; al-Bursawī calls it the rational soul or human spirit, and Elmalılı allows the soul that loves the world or the spirit. {"id": "75:26/q06", "question": "What are the tarāqī?", "turns_on": "Whether the term names the paired bones beside the throat, the throat itself, or chest bones/ribs; some descriptions overlap anatomically.", "positions": [{"id": "75:26/q06/p1", "position": "They are the paired collarbones bordering the hollow at the base of the neck.", "reasons": "Al-Layth and al-Rāghib describe each bone as joining the throat hollow to a shoulder. {"id": "75:36/q04", "question": "What does يُترك mean in this context?", "turns_on": "Ibn ʿAshur distinguishes the verb's ordinary metaphor of neglect from the contextual prospect of remaining unrevived.", "positions": [{"id": "75:36/q04/p1", "position": "It means being neglected or abandoned without care, extending the ordinary sense of leaving someone.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur says the basic verb is voluntarily parting from something, used metaphorically here for neglect without attention."}, {"id": "75:36/q04/p2", "position": "It means being left in nonexistence without revival.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur derives this contextual sense from 75:3 and 75:13 and says the question resumes the opening concern with gathering human bones."}]}
{"id": "75:36/q05", "question": "Why is يُترك passive?", "turns_on": "The sources offer different rhetorical purposes for leaving the agent unspoken.", "positions": [{"id": "75:36/q05/p1", "position": "The unnamed agent focuses attention on the imagined abandonment itself.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi says the point is being left wholly without purpose or care, regardless of who leaves one."}, {"id": "75:36/q05/p2", "position": "God's agency is already clear, so the passive is concise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur makes this point while explaining the prospect of being left without revival."}, {"id": "75:36/q05/p3", "position": "The omitted agent continues a sequence of passives and suits the sura's urgent tone.", "reasons": "Samarraʾi compares the subsequent verbs for being created, fashioned, and made with the preceding passive."}]}

{"id": "75:36/q11", "question": "How does this question connect with the surrounding sura and subsequent verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:36/q11/p1", "position": "It resumes the sura's resurrection question and leads into proof from human creation and God's power to revive.", "reasons": "Zajjaj moves from rejecting an aimless life to God's power to initiate creation at 75:37. {"id": "75:37/q07", "question": "How is يمنى read, and what does its verb agree with?", "turns_on": "Grammatical agreement with feminine nuṭfa or masculine maniyy, and whether a masculine pronoun can refer back to nuṭfa by sense.", "positions": [{"id": "75:37/q07/p1", "position": "With tāʾ, tumnā agrees with the feminine drop, nuṭfa.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī assigns it to most Medinan and Kufan readers; al-Fārisī names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, and records varying Abū ʿAmr routes.
